water.title: Little sips, all day
water.intro: Tap once for each glass — about 250 ml. Water is best, but milk and other drinks count too.
water.start: Start with a glass now — small sips count.
water.tip: Aim for about 2–2.5 litres (8–10 glasses) a day, and a little more in hot weather or when you’re active. Pale yellow pee is a good sign you’re drinking enough.
water.tipSick: If you’re being sick a lot and can’t keep fluids down, contact your midwife or doctor.

kegel.title: A few minutes for your pelvic floor
kegel.intro: Strong pelvic floor muscles help with bladder control in pregnancy and after birth. Follow the circle: squeeze as it grows, let go as it softens.
kegel.doneBody: Aim for 3 sets a day — little and often is what helps.
kegel.how1: Find the right muscles: imagine stopping yourself peeing and holding in wind. Don’t make a habit of actually stopping your flow — it’s only a way to find them.
kegel.how2: Squeeze and lift, then let go completely — relaxing matters as much as squeezing.
kegel.how3: Keep breathing normally, and try not to pull in your tummy or squeeze your bottom or thighs.
kegel.how4: Aim for 3 sets a day — lying down, sitting or standing all work.
kegel.howHelp: Not sure you’re doing them right, or noticing leaks or pain? Ask your midwife or doctor — a pelvic health physio can help.
kegel.source2: NHS — Common health problems in pregnancy
breath.title: Breathe with the circle
breath.intro: A few slow breaths can settle a busy mind. Breathe in through your nose, out through your mouth, and let your shoulders drop.
breath.doneBody: Take a moment before you get up, and notice how you feel.
breath.noteDizzy: 4-7-8 breathing can make some people feel light-headed. If you feel dizzy, stop and breathe normally.
breath.notePregnancy: Later in pregnancy, long breath-holds can feel uncomfortable — skip the holds or choose “Gentle” if that suits you better.

kick.title: Get to know your baby’s rhythm
kick.sub: Tap each time you feel a kick, swish or roll. There’s no magic number — what matters is your baby’s usual pattern.
kick.reached: 10 movements in {time}. Lovely to feel them.
kick.twoHours: It’s been 2 hours. If your baby is moving less than usual for them, call your maternity unit now.
kick.alert.title: Movements slowed, changed or stopped?
kick.alert.body: Call your maternity unit now — don’t wait until tomorrow, even if it’s the middle of the night. Don’t rely on a home heartbeat monitor.
kick.about.title: About counting
kick.about.pattern: Every baby has their own pattern of busy and quiet times. Get to know yours, and keep noticing movements every day — right up to and during labour.
kick.about.ten: Some care teams, especially in the US, suggest timing how long it takes to feel 10 movements — many people feel 10 within 2 hours. It’s a way of counting, not a test to pass. If your midwife or doctor gave you a different method, use theirs.
kick.early: First movements are usually felt between 16 and 24 weeks. If you haven’t felt any by 24 weeks, let your midwife or doctor know.

con.urgent.title: Call your maternity unit now
con.urgent.long: A contraction lasted longer than 2 minutes.
con.urgent.frequent: You’ve had 6 or more contractions in 10 minutes.
con.urgent.preterm: You’re under 37 weeks and having regular contractions.
con.rule.title: When to call: the 5-1-1 rule
con.rule.body: A common rule of thumb: contractions about 5 minutes apart, each lasting about 1 minute, for 1 hour. That’s a good time to call your maternity unit — or follow the plan they gave you.
con.rule.sooner: Call straight away, even at night, if your waters break, you have any bleeding, your baby is moving less, a contraction lasts more than 2 minutes, or you’re under 37 weeks.
con.measure: “Apart” is timed from the start of one contraction to the start of the next.

mood.low.crisis: If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, get help right away.
mood.severe.nausea: Can’t keep food or drink down? Call your midwife or GP today — severe pregnancy sickness is treatable.
mood.severe.cramps: Strong cramps that don’t ease with rest, or that come with bleeding, need checking — call your maternity unit.

ab.title: About Marigold
ab.intro: Marigold is an independent pregnancy companion. We write every article and safety entry in plain language and link each one to the public guidance it’s based on.
ab.howBody: Content is compiled from public guidance by the NHS, ACOG, WHO, CDC, FDA, NICE, RCOG, MotherToBaby and the Turkish Ministry of Health. Every entry links to its sources so you can read the original. Guidance can differ between countries — your own midwife or doctor knows you best.
ab.disclaimerBody: Marigold provides general information for education and reassurance. It is not a medical device and does not diagnose, treat or replace professional care. In an emergency, call your local emergency number.
ab.calcBody: Due date: Naegele’s rule (first day of last period + 280 days), as used by ACOG and the NHS; IVF transfers are adjusted for embryo age. Baby sizes are approximate averages. Weight-gain ranges follow the Institute of Medicine (2009). The 5-1-1 contraction guide follows ACOG patient guidance.
loss.title: Pregnancy loss support
loss.intro: We’re so sorry. If your pregnancy has ended, Marigold can pause every baby update and notification right away. Your journal and photos stay safe, and you can start a new pregnancy any time — always free.
loss.toggleSub: Hides baby development and stops all pregnancy notifications
loss.support: You don’t have to go through this alone
loss.supportBody: Talk to your midwife, doctor or GP about physical recovery and emotional support. Charities such as Tommy’s and the Miscarriage Association (UK), Share (US) offer free, kind support.
loss.newPregnancySub: Enter a new due date whenever you’re ready

loss.homeBody: Baby updates are paused. Your journal is here whenever you want it. Tap for support resources.
